passages.happening:
“You are to construct the tabernacle itself with ten curtains of finely spun linen, each with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and cherubim skillfully worked into them” (verse 1). They are joined in two sets by loops of blue and gold clasps, “so that the tabernacle will be a unit” (verses 2-6).

Over them goes a tent of eleven curtains of goat hair, joined with bronze clasps (verses 7-13). “Also make a covering for the tent out of ram skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 25 described the furniture at the heart of the sanctuary. Chapter 26 builds the house around it.

Picture the tent from the inside out. The first layer is fine linen, woven in blue, purple and scarlet, the colors of kings, with cherubim worked into the cloth. A priest standing inside would see the walls and roof alive with winged guardians, like a heavenly King's throne room. Cherubim had guarded the way to the tree of life after Eden.

Over that comes a tent of goat hair. Goat-hair cloth was the ordinary stuff of tents in the Near East: dark, rough and waterproof. Then ram skins dyed red, and over all a covering of leather.

So from outside, the tabernacle looked like a plain tent among the other tents of the camp. Its splendor was inside, seen only by those who served there.

The clasps join the curtains so that the tabernacle is ‘a unit’, one whole. The Hebrew way of saying the curtains are joined one to another is, word for word, a woman to her sister. It is the ordinary Hebrew idiom.
passages.later:
God reminded David that for all those years he had lived in a tent: “I have moved about with a tent as My dwelling” (2 Samuel 7:6).

Ezekiel saw cherubim beneath God's throne: “above the heads of the cherubim, the likeness of a throne of sapphire” (Ezekiel 10:1).

John writes that the Word “made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). The tent of these chapters stands behind that sentence.
passages.asks: The tabernacle was plain outside and glorious within. Ask whether you judge people, or churches, by what can be seen from outside. And ask what it would mean for your own life to be more beautiful within than it looks.

passages.happening:
“You are to construct upright frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle. Each frame is to be ten cubits long and a cubit and a half wide” (verses 15-16). They stand on silver bases, two under each frame, and are held together by crossbars covered with gold (verses 17-29).

“So you are to set up the tabernacle according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
The frames are the walls. Together they make a long, narrow room, about 30 cubits by 10, roughly 45 by 15 feet or 14 by 4.5 meters.

These are instructions for craftsmen, not a full drawing. So people who try to draw the tabernacle differ. Were the frames solid boards, or open frames like ladders, through which the colored linen could be seen? Solid boards that size would have been very heavy to carry. Did the tent have a peaked roof or a flat one? The text does not say, and reconstructions differ.

The metals tell a story. Bronze is used at the entrance, silver for the bases of the frames, gold for the frames and everything inside. A priest going inward passed from bronze to silver to gold: the nearer to God, the more precious.

The entrance faced east, and the inner room lay to the west. A worshiper coming toward God faced west, with the rising sun at his back.
passages.later:
Ezekiel later condemns men in the temple who turned their backs on God's house, “bowing to the east in worship of the sun” (Ezekiel 8:16). Some see in the tabernacle's direction a refusal of sun worship.

Solomon's temple kept the same plan in stone. Its inner room “was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high” (1 Kings 6:20).

Before the temple, the tent stood at Shiloh: “the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the Tent of Meeting there” (Joshua 18:1).
passages.hard:
Was the tabernacle real, or a later picture of Solomon's temple set back in the wilderness?

In the late nineteenth century Julius Wellhausen argued that the tabernacle of Exodus 25 to 40 was the Jerusalem temple made portable and set back in the time of Moses by priestly writers in or after the exile. He pointed to the rich materials, the fine craftsmanship asked of freed slaves in the desert, and a simpler ‘Tent of Meeting’ pitched outside the camp in 33:7-11. Many critical scholars still see the priestly tabernacle as at least an ideal picture shaped by later temple practice.

Others argue for an early core. They point to Egyptian portable shrines and royal camp tents. Egyptian carvings of Ramesses II's campaign against Kadesh, in the thirteenth century BC, show the king's tent inside a rectangular camp, with the throne room at the back. A gilded frame that could be taken apart, made for Queen Hetepheres, mother of Khufu, was found in her tomb at Giza. They note features that differ from Solomon's temple rather than copy it: a tent, not a stone house; goat hair and skins; acacia, not cedar. And they point to later mentions of a tent sanctuary before the temple, at Shiloh and in God's words to David.

The question remains open, and these notes take no side. The chapter's claim, that God chose to live among his people in a house he could travel in, does not depend on settling it.
passages.asks: Everything had to follow the pattern God showed. Ask whether you build your life by your own plan and then ask God to bless it, or by his. And ask what it means that God chose a house that could move with his people wherever they went.

passages.happening:
“Make a veil of blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen, with cherubim skillfully worked into it” (verse 31). It hangs on four gold-covered posts (verse 32).

“And hang the veil from the clasps and place the ark of the Testimony behind the veil. So the veil will separate the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place” (verse 33). The mercy seat goes on the ark in the Most Holy Place (verse 34). The table stands outside the veil on the north side, and the lampstand opposite it on the south (verse 35).

A curtain of the same colors closes the entrance to the tent (verses 36-37).
passages.hearers:
Now God places each piece in its room. Behind the veil, in the Most Holy Place, the ark with its mercy seat. In front of the veil, in the Holy Place, the table on one side and the lampstand on the other.

Most drawings make the Most Holy Place a perfect cube of ten cubits, as the inner room of Solomon's temple was a cube.

The veil, paroket in Hebrew, is the most solemn boundary in Israel's worship. It hid the ark from sight. Cherubim were woven into it, guarding God's presence as they had guarded Eden. Only the high priest would pass through it, once a year, on the Day of Atonement.

The veil was not a wall of hostility. It was a mercy as well as a barrier. God was near, in the middle of the camp, and the veil kept those who served close by from being consumed by his holiness.
passages.later:
Leviticus gives the rule: Aaron is “not to enter freely into the Most Holy Place behind the veil in front of the mercy seat on the ark, or else he will die” (Leviticus 16:2).

Hebrews reads the shape of the tent: “the way into the Most Holy Place had not yet been disclosed as long as the first tabernacle was still standing” (Hebrews 9:8). It speaks of “the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (Hebrews 10:20).

When Jesus died, “the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom” (Mark 15:38).

Hebrews does not make Israel's worship empty. As its notes on this site say, a shadow is real. It has the true shape of what casts it, and God truly met his people in the tent.
passages.asks: The veil kept the way to God's presence closed, and the Gospels say it was torn from top to bottom. Ask whether you come to God as if the way were still shut. And ask what it means that the opening came from God's side.
